title: Concerns raised over AI monitoring tool in Mental Health hospitals
source_used: Channel 4 News (written version of Ayshah Tull's report, channel4news.substack.com, 13 Oct 2026); BBC (6 Oct 2026) for the inquiry background
key_facts: Channel 4 News health correspondent Ayshah Tull reports that Oxevision, an AI-powered camera monitoring system, is used in about half of NHS mental health trusts in England to monitor patients in their bedrooms.
It is being scrutinised at the Lampard Inquiry, the public inquiry into mental health patient deaths in Essex, over consent, privacy, dignity and human rights, and whether it replaces trained staff.
The company behind it, LIO Health, has acknowledged limitations in evidence to the inquiry and says it supports an explicit consent model and that Oxevision was never designed to replace nurses.
LIO Health says it makes the technology and does not tell organisations how to use it.
A screen shows each patient bed in green, yellow or red depending on the alert, and video taken for 15 seconds is used to measure pulse and breathing rate.

The inquiry has heard that four people who died had Oxevision mentioned in their inquests; for one of them, 16-year-old Elise Sebastian, staff did not adequately check on her and her monitor was muted.

BBC (6 Oct 2026): NHS England told the inquiry that a review found 10 mental health trusts were not running their consent processes in line with its digital principles, and it passed this to the Care Quality Commission on 2 Oct.
quote_evidence: The company behind an AI-powered monitoring system used in NHS mental health hospitals has acknowledged limitations in evidence to a public inquiry.
But a camera monitoring system called Oxevision is being used in half of NHS mental health trusts in England to capture images inside a patient’s bedroom.

why_it_matters_hint: Patients detained in mental health wards may be filmed in their bedrooms, and families say consent and human care are being sidelined, while the maker says it saves lives.
